procedural_history.originating_court: Judicial Magistrate, First Class, second court, Bijapur
procedural_history.impugned_order: Orders of acquittal in three separate cases for offences punishable under s. 29(1)(d) of the Mysore Sales Tax Act, 1957.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The State of Mysore appealed the orders of acquittal to the Mysore High Court. The High Court rejected the appeals, stating that the State had other remedies under the Act to enforce payment and did not deem it fit to exercise its discretion under s. 421 (I) of the Code of Criminal Procedure to entertain the appeals.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the High Court's judgment and order dated March 17, 1965, in Criminal Appeals Nos. 93 to 95 of 1965.

decision.conviction_status: Acquittal of the respondent in the three cases set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether the mere filing of an appeal against an assessment order, without obtaining a specific stay from the appellate authority, suspends the liability to pay the assessed tax, thereby making a prosecution for non-payment of tax under Section 29(1)(d) of the Mysore Sales Tax Act, 1957, not maintainable.

facts: The respondent was assessed for sales tax and served a notice to pay the amount within 21 days.
He filed an appeal against the assessment order but did not pay the tax.
Crucially, the respondent did not obtain an order from the appellate authority to stay the proceedings for tax recovery.
While the appeal was pending, a criminal complaint was filed against him under Section 29(1)(d) of the Mysore Sales Tax Act, 1957, for non-payment of the tax.
The trial court and the High Court acquitted him, believing the pending appeal made the prosecution invalid.

law.provision: Section 20(5) of the Mysore Sales Tax Act, 1957
law.explanation: This section explicitly states that even if an appeal has been filed, the tax must be paid in accordance with the assessment. It allows the appellate authority to give directions regarding payment (i.e., grant a stay), but this is discretionary and not automatic.
This section makes it a punishable offense for an assessee to fail to pay the tax within the time allowed.

This section outlines methods for the *recovery* of unpaid tax. Its proviso protects an assessee from these recovery methods *if* they have obtained and complied with a stay order from an appellate authority.

application: The Court held that the liability to pay tax is created by the assessment order itself and is not automatically suspended just because an appeal has been filed.
The Court pointed to the clear and specific language of Section 20(5), which mandates that the tax must be paid "Notwithstanding that an appeal has been preferred".

The only way for an assessee to get interim relief from the obligation to pay is to obtain a specific stay order from the appellate authority, as provided for in the proviso to Section 20(5). The respondent failed to do this.

The Court clarified that the proviso to Section 13(3) only provides protection from specific *recovery* proceedings (like treating the tax as an arrear of land revenue) and is not a defense against a *prosecution* for the offense of non-payment under Section 29(1)(d).
Therefore, when the respondent did not pay the tax within the time specified in the demand notice, he committed the offense under Section 29(1)(d), regardless of his pending appeal.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the respondent's argument, concluding that the mere filing of an appeal, without obtaining a specific stay order from the appellate authority, does not suspend the liability to pay the assessed tax. Consequently, the prosecution for non-payment of tax under Section 29(1)(d) was maintainable.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the mere filing of an appeal against an assessment order, without obtaining a specific stay from the appellate authority, suspends the liability to pay the assessed tax, thereby making a prosecution for non-payment of tax under Section 29(1)(d) of the Mysore Sales Tax Act, 1957, not maintainable.
appellant_arguments: The filing of an appeal does not suspend the liability to pay tax, as explicitly stated by Section 20(5) of the Mysore Sales Tax Act, 1957, which provides that 'Notwithstanding that an appeal has been preferred under sub-section (I), the tax shall be paid in accordance with the assessment made in the case'.
The respondent's failure to pay the tax was a deliberate and therefore 'wilful' act, as he knew he was required to pay within a certain time and had not complied with the notice of demand.
This wilful failure to pay is an offence under Section 29(1)(d) of the Act, and the prosecution was therefore warranted.
respondent_arguments: The liability of the assessee to pay the tax must be deemed to have been suspended during the pendency of the appeal against the assessment order.
There was no 'wilful default' on the part of the respondent in not paying the tax.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A deliberate failure to pay a tax, with the knowledge of the requirement to pay within a certain time, constitutes a 'wilful default'. The obligation to pay an assessed tax is not automatically suspended by the filing of an appeal; the tax must be paid unless the appellate authority directs otherwise.
obiter: The court's speculation that the State's undertaking not to prosecute the respondent likely meant they would not press for a conviction and sentence.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The mere filing of an appeal against an assessment order does not suspend the assessee's liability to pay the tax. The liability is created by the order of assessment itself, and Section 20(5) of the Mysore Sales Tax Act, 1957, explicitly mandates that the tax shall be paid notwithstanding the appeal. A deliberate failure to pay the tax within the time allowed, even with a pending appeal, is a 'wilful' act and constitutes an offence under Section 29(1)(d) of the Act.
legal_tests_applied: Statutory Interpretation of Section 20(5): The court applied a plain reading of the statute, which states, 'Notwithstanding that an appeal has been preferred under sub-section (I), the tax shall be paid in accordance with the assessment made in the case'.

Definition of 'Wilful Default': The court defined a 'wilful' act as one that is deliberate. It found that because the respondent knew he was required to pay the tax within a certain time and knew he had not complied, his failure to pay was 'quite clearly deliberate and, therefore, wilful.'

Statutory Interpretation of Section 13(3) Proviso: The court interpreted this proviso not as a bar to prosecution, but as a provision that 'afforded interim protection from action under cl. (a) or cl. (b) provided that he approaches the appropriate authority and obtains from that authority an order of stay of proceedings'. It does not negate the underlying liability or the offence of non-payment.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's argument that the liability to pay tax was suspended during the appeal was rejected because it 'ignores the specific provisions of sub-s. (5) of s. 20'.

The respondent's contention that there was no 'wilful default' was rejected on the grounds that 'The respondent knew that he was required to pay the tax within certain time and also knew that he had not complied with the notice of demand. His action in not paying the tax was quite clearly deliberate and, therefore, wilful.'

The respondent's reliance on the proviso to Section 13(3) as a defense against prosecution was rejected, with the court stating, 'we fail to see how the proviso to sub-s. (3) of s. 13 can at all be an answer to a prosecution under s. 29 (!) (d). What is rendered an offence under s. 29 (I) (d) is the failure of the assessee to pay the tax within the time allowed.'
policy_considerations: The final disposition of not convicting or sentencing the respondent was not based on legal reasoning or public policy, but on a specific 'undertaking was given by the State that irrespective of the result of the appeal the respondent would not be prosecuted.'
